# Abstract


Understanding the population dynamics of Antarctic krill (*Euphausia superba*) is fundamental for ecosystem-based fisheries management in the Western Antarctic Peninsula (WAP), where environmental variability and predator–prey interactions strongly influence population productivity. Most stock assessment frameworks treat ecosystem drivers as external to the core population dynamics, limiting their influence on estimated stock status and management advice. Here, a spatially implicit integrated length-to-age model is applied to Antarctic krill within a Stock Synthesis framework, evaluating four alternative configurations in which environmental covariates and predator indices are either embedded within the structural equations governing recruitment and natural mortality, or excluded. When ecosystem drivers are incorporated, lower and more conservative estimates of recruitment, spawning stock biomass, and fishing mortality are consistently obtained. Ecosystem-informed models also exhibit poorer statistical performance (higher RMSE, more pronounced retrospective patterns, and more structured residuals) interpreted as the informational and structural cost of imposing ecological constraints on a data-limited system, rather than as evidence against the relevance of the mechanisms themselves. These results indicate that assessments excluding ecosystem processes may overestimate population productivity and stock status. Predator and environmental effects can be consistently embedded within the core population dynamics of an integrated krill assessment, providing a more precautionary and ecologically realistic basis for management advice aligned with CCAMLR's conservation objectives for the WAP.


*Keywords: Antarctic krill, population dynamics, length-to-age model, stock assessment, ecosystem drivers, model diagnostics, CCAMLR*


\newpage

# Introduction

Antarctic krill (*Euphausia superba*, hereafter krill) constitutes one of the largest populations on the planet in terms of biomass and serves as a keystone species in the Antarctic ecosystem [@Atkinson2019a; @McBride2021; @Kawaguchi2024]. The population is predominantly concentrated in the Western Antarctic Peninsula (WAP), being the primary area for krill harvesting over the past four decades and also an area that is a critical feeding ground for predators such as penguins, seals, and whales [@Watters2013; @Hill2016; @Gallagher2023a]. At the same time, the WAP is one of the regions most severely affected by climate change, experiencing rapid increases in ocean temperature, sea ice loss, and shifts in primary productivity [@Turner2005; @Lima2013; @Atkinson2019a; @Morley2020; @Carrasco2021; @McBride2021]. These overlapping pressures have intensified scientific interest in understanding krill population dynamics from both an ecological and a fisheries perspective in such a complex and rapidly changing environment [@Warwick-Evans2022; @Kawaguchi2024].

Given the importance of krill to the ecosystem and its commercial value, effective management of krill stocks is essential for maintaining the balance of the Antarctic ecosystem while supporting sustainable fisheries. Recognizing this, the Commission for the Conservation of Antarctic Marine Living Resources (CCAMLR)  has been developing a revised ecosystem-based management approach for the krill fishery, known as the new Krill Fishery Management Strategy (KFMA) [@Constable2011; @Watters2013; @Cavanagh2016; @Constable2023; @Zhao2023; @Kawaguchi2024]. This strategy seeks to balance commercial harvesting with a precautionary framework that safeguards krill-dependent species across spatial and temporal scales. It comprises three key components: (i) stock assessments to establish precautionary harvest rates, (ii) periodic updates of krill biomass estimates at multiple spatial scales, and (iii) spatial overlap analysis to guide the allocation of catches and mitigate ecosystem-wide risks [@Warwick-Evans2022; @Kawaguchi2024].

To provide scientific advice on the status and abundance of krill, CCAMLR has historically relied on dedicated scientific surveys [@Watters2013; @Hill2019; @Dornam2021; @Green2023]. However, changes in survey design-both methodological and spatial-have raised concerns about the reliability of these estimates, while the high costs associated with such surveys have further motivated the search for alternative stock estimation methods. More recently, and as part of the discussions on the implementation of the KFMA, CCAMLR has explored a variety of model-based (indirect) approaches to assess krill stock status and support fisheries management decisions [@Hill2019]. Some of these stock assessment models have used a single source of data-either fishery-dependent catches [@Wang2021] or survey-based monitoring programs [@Kinzey2011; @Kinzey2019; @Green2023]. At present, the Generalized Yield Model (GRYM) [@Maschette2020] is a model-based approach used by CCAMLR to generate management recommendations, allowing adjustments to the decision rules to predefined catch limits set by CCAMLR [@Constable2000; @CCAMLR2010; @CCAMLR2021a]. However, model-based approaches exhibit important limitations, including the effective integration of multiple data sources, the incorporation of ecosystem-level variables into population dynamics, and the capacity to account for the high spatial and temporal variability intrinsic to krill productivity [@Meyer2020; @Trathan2021].

Increasing evidence demonstrates that environmental conditions, such as sea surface temperature, sea ice extent, and phytoplankton availability, strongly influence krill recruitment, survival, and spatial distribution [@Murphy2007; @Flores2012; @Saba2014; @Morley2020; @Perry2020; @Walsh2020; @Vorrath2020; @Veytia2021]. Similarly, fluctuations in predator abundance and distribution can exert significant top-down control on krill populations [@Moosa2017; @Reisinger2022; @Baines2022; @Riaz2023; @Biuw2024]. There is now broad scientific consensus on the need for stock assessment models that incorporate multiple data sources, capture temporal and spatial variability, and explicitly account for ecosystem interactions [@Marshall2019]. Neglecting these ecosystem drivers can lead to biased estimates of stock status and suboptimal management advice [@Haltuch2009; @Richards2016; @Marshall2019; @Crone2019; @Robertson2024]. Stock assessment frameworks aligned with CCAMLR's new strategy should therefore explicitly incorporate these ecosystem components to more accurately represent krill population processes.

Integrating ecological complexity into krill stock assessments presents multiple challenges. Long-term data collection is frequently affected by changes in monitoring programs and sampling methodologies [@Hill2019], and some key regions of the WAP lack sufficient temporal coverage to construct reliable population indices. Indirect ecosystem drivers, such as environmental variability and predator–prey interactions, are particularly difficult to quantify, given the spatial and temporal heterogeneity of krill dynamics, their non-linear responses to environmental forcing, and the simultaneous influence of multiple stressors [@Constable2023]. These constraints have historically limited the structural complexity of krill assessments and the degree to which ecosystem processes are embedded within their core population dynamics. Despite these challenges, a substantial and diverse body of data on krill and their associated environment has accumulated over several decades. Fishery monitoring programs provide detailed biological data from catches through onboard scientific observers, notably through CCAMLR's Scheme of International Scientific Observation (SISO). Hydroacoustic biomass surveys, primarily led by the United States and China, represent the longest-running and spatially broadest independent assessment efforts in the Southern Ocean [@Hill2019; @Dornam2021; @Green2023]. Ecosystem monitoring programs such as the CCAMLR Ecosystem Monitoring Program (CEMP) systematically assess predator populations and environmental variability at key sites across the WAP. Together, these complementary data streams provide the informational foundation needed to move beyond data-limited, single-source assessments toward integrated frameworks that explicitly account for the coupled biological, ecological, and fishery processes shaping krill populations.

CCAMLR has traditionally relied on assessments conducted within a data-limited context using relatively simple model-based approaches, such as GRYM models, which do not explicitly incorporate environmental or ecological variables in the representation of population dynamics. In contrast, a wide range of integrated assessment frameworks now allow the incorporation of diverse data sources and increasing levels of structural complexity. These include spatially explicit approaches such as the State-Space Assessment Model (SAM) [@Nielsen2021] and the Globally Applicable Area-Disaggregated General Ecosystem Toolbox (Gadget) [@Bartolino2011]. For statistical catch-at-age assessments, widely used frameworks include the C++ Algorithmic Stock Assessment Laboratory (CASAL) [@Bull2004] and Stock Synthesis (SS3) [@Methot2013], among others. Notably, Stock Synthesis can also be applied to species that are difficult to age, such as Antarctic krill, through integrated length-to-age transformation models that explicitly link observed length compositions to underlying age-structured population dynamics. These advanced tools provide robust and flexible methodologies to address data limitations while accommodating complex biological processes and ecosystem interactions, thereby enabling a more realistic representation of population dynamics and improved scientific support for ecosystem-based fisheries management [@Hoyle2020].

This study pursues two main objectives. The first is to integrate multiple data sources on Antarctic krill (*Euphausia superba*), including fishery operations (e.g., catches and effort distribution), biological characteristics (e.g., growth rates and reproductive parameters), spatiotemporal population dynamics, and key ecosystem drivers (e.g., environmental forcing and predator–prey interactions), into a unified stock assessment framework. Specifically, we apply an integrated length-to-age model that enables the explicit inclusion of environmental covariates affecting biomass, recruitment patterns, and overall productivity, as well as the potential influence of predator populations through the configuration of natural mortality. The second objective is to evaluate the performance of alternative model configurations representing different hypotheses regarding ecosystem influences, using diagnostic tools and performance metrics commonly applied in contemporary stock assessments. Consistent with CCAMLR's ecosystem-based management framework [@Constable2011; @Cavanagh2016; @Hill2019; @Constable2023; @Zhao2023; @CCAMLRWGSAM2024; @WGEMM2024], this approach provides empirical evidence of the value of ecosystem-informed assessment models, demonstrating that the incorporation of environmental and predator covariates influences population variables, model fit, predictive skill, and structural uncertainty, with implications for precautionary and sustainable management advice for the Antarctic krill fishery.

\newpage

# Methodology

## Study Area

The study area covers the WAP, corresponding to FAO Statistical Subarea 48.1. To enhance the spatial resolution of the analysis of krill population dynamics, five Management Units (MUs) proposed by CCAMLR were used: Bransfield Strait, Elephant Island, Gerlache Strait, Joinville Island, and the Southwest sector [@Dornam2021] (Figure \@ref(fig:studyarea)). Although these management units were not originally designed to incorporate krill biological or population-specific characteristics [@Watters2013; @Constable2023; @Zaldua2024a], their subdivision allows for finer-scale examination of krill data, enhancing spatial resolution and facilitating the identification of heterogeneity among different data sources, including fishery-dependent and environmental information, thereby supporting a more detailed characterization of krill population dynamics. To represent spatial heterogeneity in krill dynamics [@Perry2019; @Perry2020; @Reiss2020; @Veytia2021; @SantaCruz2022; @Mardones2026], we implemented a spatially implicit modeling approach based on the "areas-as-fleets" framework [@Waterhouse2014; @Punt2019; @Nielsen2021], in which each MU is treated as a distinct fleet with independently estimated selectivity, catchability (*q*), and abundance indices. Although MUs were treated as separate fleets for observational purposes, core population processes (recruitment, growth, and a single annual spawning pulse between January and February [@Perry2019; @McBride2021]) were modeled collectively, representing the krill stock as a single interconnected population within Subarea 48.1. Survey indices and biological compositions (e.g., length-frequency data) were assigned to their corresponding MU based on sampling location [@Dornam2021]; fishery-dependent data were stratified by MU according to reported fishing effort. This disaggregated observation structure captures regional variability without requiring explicit movement modeling [@Punt2019].

## Length-to-Age Model Description

Like many invertebrates, krill present challenges for age determination, which complicates modeling population dynamics. Most modern stock assessments rely on age-structured modeling approaches to estimate marine population parameters [@Punt2013]. Although recent advances have improved krill aging techniques [@Kilada2017], such methods have historically been unavailable for krill. Consequently, stock assessment for krill typically uses length data to approximate age structure through transition matrices. These matrices estimate the probability that individuals of a given length belong to specific age classes [@Laslett2004; @Lee2019; @Rudd2021; @Zhang2022; @Lee2024]. Given the scarcity or absence of direct age data in krill monitoring programs, length-based models offer a practical alternative to age-structured approaches. To date, all model-based krill assessments have used length-to-age frameworks [@Kinzey2015; @Kinzey2019; @Wang2021; @Green2023; @Zhang2022]. Integrated models can effectively capture age structure by transforming length observations into population-level dynamics [@Punt2013; @Lee2024]. Length data, which are cost-effective and readily available [@Chong2019; @Canales2021], also provide valuable insights into krill population structure due to their correlation with age [@Thanassekos2014].

To perform this transformation, models typically use Age-Length Keys (ALKs). An ALK is a probabilistic matrix that estimates the likelihood of individuals of a given length belonging to specific age classes. This method assumes that both aged and measured individuals are random samples from the same population and should be applied within the same time period to avoid biases [@ICCA2003; @Punt2003; @Punt2013; @Lee2024]. Using this statistical framework, we constructed the ALK for Antarctic krill, which was subsequently applied within the assessment model. In the catch-at-length stock assessment model, growth was parameterized using a von Bertalanffy growth function (VBGF) for length-at-age. This formulation was integrated with the weight-at-length relationship, which was assumed known and derived from the parameters reported by @Maschette2020 for Antarctic krill. To account for early ontogeny, linear growth was assumed below a predefined settlement age of 1.5 years. Maturity was modeled as an age-based logistic function, with the onset of maturity occurring between 2 and 3 years [@Thanassekos2014]. Fishery selectivity was represented by a logistic function parameterized by the length at 50% selectivity ($L_{50}$) and the selection range ($L_{95}$), estimated independently for each MU to account for spatial differences in size-dependent catchability. Survey selectivity was modeled using the same logistic formulation, likewise estimated separately per MU. Allowing fleet and survey, and MU-specific selectivity curves is particularly important for krill, where spatial variation in size composition, driven by environmental gradients and population structure, can produce systematic differences in the size of individuals encountered by different fleets and in different regions (S1 Fig. 11). 

The stock-recruitment (SR) relationship was modeled using a Beverton–Holt function (S2, Eq. 7), following @Kinzey2019. The steepness parameter was fixed at 0.85 to maintain consistency with previous studies, reflecting the weak relationship between spawning biomass and recruitment in krill populations, where recruitment is largely driven by environmental variability [@Dong2025; @Kinzey2019; @Perry2020]. Unfished recruitment ($R_0$) was estimated assuming a mean recruitment of 23 mm (log-scale), with a prior of 10. Recruitment deviations were included to capture interannual variability using the deviation vector approach (*recdev = 1*), whereby recruitment is modeled as a function of spawning stock biomass plus a deviation term. Cyclic recruitment patterns were also incorporated, assuming periodicity at three- and five-year intervals [@Perry2019; @McBride2021; @Kinzey2019; @Thanassekos2014]. All life-history parameters and assumptions were specified as priors to define the initial population dynamics, based on data from @Smith2023a, @Maschette2020, and @Kinzey2011. These biological parameters, together with the initial selectivity assumptions, are summarized in Table S2, Table 1.

The statistical model for krill was configured using Stock Synthesis v3.30.21 (SS3) [@Methot2013]. SS3 is a structured stock assessment model belonging to the class of integrated stock assessment models, with a set of sub-models that simulate growth, maturity, fecundity, recruitment, and mortality processes, along with observation sub-models that generate expected values for different data types. The model is coded in Automatic Differentiation Model Builder (ADMB) [@Fournier2012; @Methot2013; @methot2020stock] with estimated parameters. SS3 model configuration files are available in the code repository (Supplementary Material 1). All modeling analyses were conducted in R version 4.4.2 [@R-base], with visualization and diagnostics performed through *r4ss* [@Taylor2019] and *ss3diags* [@Winker2023] packages. The complete set of equations governing population dynamics, selectivity, stock-recruitment, mortality, and parameter estimation within the SS3 framework are detailed in Supplementary Material 2.

## Environmental Link Formulation

Within the Stock Synthesis (SS3) framework, environmental covariates influence population dynamics through link functions applied to underlying model parameters (e.g., recruitment, natural mortality, or growth), rather than acting directly on observed quantities [@methot2020stock; @Caserta2025]. These parameter-level effects propagate to derived quantities such as annual recruitment. Let $P_t$ denote a generic model parameter influenced by the environment, $P_{base}$ its baseline value under average environmental conditions, $E_t$ the environmental covariate, and $\beta_E$ the estimable coefficient describing environmental sensitivity. Chlorophyll-a (Chl-a) was selected as the environmental covariate based on its well-documented influence on krill population dynamics in the Western Antarctic Peninsula [@Flores2012; @Morley2020; @Veytia2021; @Walsh2020], and its demonstrated effect on krill recruitment productivity specifically confirmed by @Saba2014 and @Mardones2025. Chl-a was obtained from a combination of satellite products including *Nimbus-7* and the *EU Copernicus Marine Service* (S1. Fig 1). Prior to model fitting, the Chl-a time series was standardised to zero mean and unit variance:

$$E_t = \frac{C_t - \bar{C}}{\sigma_C}$$

where $C_t$ is the raw annual Chl-a concentration (mg m$^{-3}$), and $\bar{C}$ and $\sigma_C$ are the historical mean and standard deviation. This standardisation improves numerical stability, renders $\beta_E$ interpretable as the change in the target parameter per one standard deviation anomaly in Chl-a, and is consistent with recommended practice in SS3 [@methot2020stock] (S1. Fig 2). Under this formulation, the environmental link captures interannual variability in recruitment relative to the long-term baseline $\ln(R_0)_{base}$. The environmental effect was implemented via an additive link (link type 2 in SS3) [@Caserta2025]:

$$P_t = P_{\text{base}} + \beta_E \cdot E_t$$

where $\beta_E$ is estimated freely within the model. For years with missing Chl-a observations, SS3 assigns $E_t = 0$, effectively reverting the parameter to its baseline value [@methot2020stock].

## Predator Modelling

Predation is incorporated in SS3 through an additional mortality component ($M_2$), augmenting background natural mortality ($M_1$) [@methot2020stock]. This approach enables partial representation of ecosystem processes within a single-species framework, in contrast to fully dynamic ecosystem models such as ATLANTIS or Ecopath with Ecosim [@fulton2003; @fulton2011; @christensen2004]. Total instantaneous mortality is defined as:

$$Z_{a,t} = M1_{a,t} + \sum_i M2_{a,t,i} + F_{a,t}$$

where $M2_{a,t,i}$ represents predation mortality from predator $i$. In our krill assessment, predation pressure was represented using the three penguin species in the Antarctic Peninsula: Adélie (*Pygoscelis adeliae*), Chinstrap (*Pygoscelis antarcticus*), and Gentoo (*Pygoscelis papua*), whose annual abundance was obtained from 399 colonies monitored over the period 2000–2020 through the Mapping Application for Penguin Populations and Projected Dynamics ([MAPPPD](https://www.penguinmap.com/mapppd/sources/)) [@Oceanites2021]. Penguin abundance was aggregated across species and used as a combined predator index. Length-frequency distributions of krill from penguin stomach contents, used to characterise predator size selectivity, were obtained from the U.S.AMLR Scientific Research Program (AMLR), with data available from 1992 onwards (S1. Fig 3). The predator component was implemented as a dedicated fleet within SS3, combining two observational data streams: (i) the aggregated penguin abundance index, used to inform time-varying predation mortality, and (ii) the annual krill length-frequency distributions from stomach contents, used to estimate predator selectivity. Predation mortality was parameterized as:

$$M2_{a,t} = Q \times I_{pred,t}$$

where $I_{pred,t}$ is the standardized predator index and $Q$ is an estimable scaling parameter, analogous to catchability in fishing mortality [@methot2020stock]. The term $M2_{a,t}$ was further parameterised as a time-varying quantity via annual log-scale deviations with a zero-reverting logit-link random walk (dev\_link = 5 in SS3), which constrains $M2_{a,t}$ within biologically plausible bounds across the time series. Diet composition data, in the form of annual length-frequency distributions of krill from penguin stomach contents, informed the size-selectivity function of predation. Parameters were estimated within SS3 using the stomach content length data as the observational likelihood component for the predator fleet, allowing the model to reconcile abundance and diet data streams during estimation [@methot2020stock]. Model diagnostics for predation focus on the relative contribution of predation to total mortality, summarized by the ratio $M2/Z$, as well as the shape of the estimated selectivity function, which reveals size-dependent predation patterns. The M2 framework relies on simplifying assumptions, including the absence of predator–prey feedbacks, a linear functional response between predator abundance and predation mortality, and the use of population averaged selectivity.

## Data Sources


In addition to the predator and environmental covariates described above, the model was informed primarily by fishery-dependent and fishery-independent monitoring data. Fishery-dependent data were obtained from the CCAMLR Scheme of International Scientific Observation (SISO) and comprised total catch in weight, standardized catch-per-unit-effort (CPUE, grouped by vessel, area, and depth, 1997–2020 across MUs, which served as a fishery-based relative abundance index complementing survey-derived biomass estimates, and krill length-frequency distributions (detailed below). Fishery-independent data came from U.S. AMLR Program acoustic surveys, providing standardized biomass indices by MU between 1991 and 2011 [@Dornam2021] (S1, Fig. 4). Biological sampling was discontinued after that period, reflecting the AMLR programme's transition toward autonomous underwater vehicle glider-based acoustic surveys [@Reiss2021], which do not generate length-frequency data. This gap does not substantially compromise the assessment, since the AMLR biological series spans the full range of observed environmental and fishing conditions, providing sufficient temporal coverage to reliably estimate growth, selectivity, and size-structure dynamics that propagate into subsequent model years through the population dynamics equations. Length-frequency data used in the model were drawn from three independent sources, each reflecting a distinct sampling context. SISO compositions (2000–2020) represent krill sampled during commercial fishing operations by MU; coverage is spatially and temporally uneven, since no samples are available for MU-years without commercial activity. AMLR survey compositions (1991–2011) reflect the size structure encountered by standardized scientific trawls. Predator-derived compositions come from stomach content analyses of krill predators monitored under the AMLR programme (1977–2020, with the 2000–2020 subset used in this analysis), providing an independent, ecologically informative signal of krill body size dynamics. All three sources were standardized to a common bin structure of 28 intervals (0.2 cm width, lower edges from 1.2 to 6.6 cm), ensuring consistency across years, MUs, and fleets (fishery, survey, predator) for reliable temporal and spatial comparison of size structure (S1, Fig. 4). All data described here and in the previous section, together with their temporal coverage and spatial scale, are summarized in Table \@ref(tab:data-sources).

## Scenarios

A set of model configurations was evaluated, incorporating variations in predator "fleet" and environmental effects, and their impacts on spawning biomass, recruitment, and other population variables. The methodology involves assessing the statistical performance of the model under these configurations.  Specifically, s1.1 serves as the reference model, incorporating only fishery and survey data while accounting for spatial heterogeneity (implicit spatial model). The subsequent scenarios build upon this configuration to evaluate the effects of additional ecological components. s1.2 extends s1.1 by incorporating predator influences, allowing the model to assess the impact of predation on krill population dynamics. s1.3 modifies s1.1 by introducing chlorophyll-a as an environmental covariate, capturing potential environmental drivers of recruitment. Finally, s1.4 integrates both predator and environmental influences into the s1.1 framework, providing a more complete representation of ecosystem interactions and their role in krill population dynamics. Regarding spatial heterogeneity, this approach was considered in all scenarios (Table \@ref(tab:scenario)).

```{r scenario, eval=TRUE}
scenario_table <- data.frame(
  Scenario    = c("s1.1", "s1.2", "s1.3", "s1.4"),
  Description = c(
    "Base model",
    "Base model + predator mortality",
    "Base model + environmental covariate",
    "Base model + predator mortality + environmental covariate"
  ),
  Predator    = c("No", "Yes", "No",  "Yes"),
  Environment = c("No", "No",  "Yes", "Yes"),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

ft_scenarios <- flextable(scenario_table) |>
  set_header_labels(
    Scenario    = "Scenario",
    Description = "Description",
    Predator    = "Predator (M\u2082)",
    Environment = "Chl-a link"
  ) |>
  set_caption("Model configurations evaluated for Antarctic krill stock assessment.") |>
  theme_booktabs() |>
  fontsize(size = 10, part = "all") |>
  bold(part = "header") |>
  align(j = c("Predator", "Environment"), align = "center", part = "all") |>
  autofit() |>
  set_table_properties(width = 1, layout = "autofit")

ft_scenarios
```

## Model Diagnostics

Performance evaluation and scenario comparison for the krill stock assessment followed the framework proposed by @Carvalho2017, @Carvalho2021b, @Merino2022a, and @Kell2021, combining measures of estimation stability, goodness-of-fit, retrospective consistency, and predictive skill to evaluate the reliability and robustness of the results across the four modeling scenarios (s1.1–s1.4). Convergence of the estimation algorithm was assessed for each scenario by reviewing parameter trace plots, the gradient of the objective function, and the positive-definiteness of the Hessian matrix, to confirm that all parameters reached a stable solution. Model fit to the observed data (catch, survey indices, and length composition) was evaluated by comparing observed and predicted values. Standardized Pearson residuals, calculated as the difference between observed and expected values divided by the expected standard deviation, were examined for the predicted length distributions across the four scenarios to detect systematic biases by size class and data source. Residual randomness for each abundance-index and length-composition series was additionally tested using the runs test, with the associated p-value computed for each series and scenario. Temporal structure in recruitment residuals was assessed through the autocorrelation function (ACF) of annual recruitment deviations across scenarios [@jhonson2016]; significant autocorrelation at successive lags indicates residual temporal structure not captured by the estimated stock-recruitment relationship. Total likelihood and its major components (survey index and length composition) were compared across scenarios together with the number of estimated parameters, to characterize relative differences in model fit prior to the AIC-based comparison described below. Retrospective consistency was evaluated by sequentially removing the terminal five years of data and re-fitting each scenario, following @HurtadoF2015. As part of this analysis, Mohn's rho ($\rho_M$) was calculated as the mean relative difference between the peeled and reference (full-data) estimates of the quantity of interest, for each retrospective peel $y = 1, ..., h$:


$$
\rho_M = \frac{1}{h} \sum_{y=1}^{h} \left( \frac{X_{T - y} - \hat{X}_{T - y}}{\hat{X}_{T - y}} \right)
$$

where $X$ represents the quantities of interest (spawning stock biomass, SSB, or fishing mortality, F), $\hat{X}$ is the corresponding estimate from the reference model fitted to the full dataset, $T$ refers to the terminal assessment year, and $h$ denotes the number of retrospective peels. One-step-ahead forecast bias was computed analogously, comparing each peel's one-year-ahead forecast against the corresponding estimate from the reference model, and is reported alongside Mohn's rho as Forecast Rho. Also, predictive skill, independent of retrospective bias, was assessed through hindcast cross-validation on the same five retrospective peels, comparing one-step-ahead hindcast predictions against observed data using the Mean Absolute Scaled Error (MASE), which scales the model's mean absolute forecast error relative to that of a naïve random-walk baseline. A MASE > 1 indicates that the model predicts no better than a random walk; MASE < 1 indicates genuine predictive skill; and MASE = 1 denotes equivalence with the naïve baseline.

Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE) values were extracted from the variance-tuning diagnostics of each scenario for the abundance indices and length-composition data, and compared across scenarios as percentage change relative to the baseline configuration (s1.1). Model performance was also evaluated using the Akaike Information Criterion (AIC) [@Bozdogan1987], which balances model fit and complexity, facilitating comparisons across scenarios. This metric penalizes model fit by twice the number of estimated parameters ($\text{AIC} = -2\ln\mathcal{L} + 2k$), thereby discouraging overparameterization [@Akaike1974]. Lower AIC values indicate more parsimonious models with better overall fit. Table \@ref(tab:metrics) summarizes the diagnostic metrics used to evaluate model performance.

```{r metrics, eval=TRUE}
df_model_metrics <- data.frame(
  Metric = c(
    "Pearson Residuals",
    "Root Mean Square Error (RMSE)",
    "Mean Absolute Scaled Error (MASE)",
    "Akaike Information Criterion (AIC)",
    "Mohn's Rho (SSB and F)",
    "Forecast Rho (SSB and F)",
    "ACF of Recruitment Deviations"
  ),
  Description = c(
    "Standardized residuals calculated as the difference between observed and expected values, divided by the standard deviation of the expected values. Useful for assessing model fit across data points.",
    "Measures the average magnitude of the residuals (prediction errors), giving higher weight to large errors. Lower values indicate better predictive accuracy.",
    "A scale-independent measure of prediction accuracy. It compares forecast errors to the errors from a naive baseline model. Values <1 indicate better-than-baseline performance.",
    "A relative measure of model quality that balances model fit and complexity. Lower AIC values indicate better models, penalizing overfitting.",
    "The mean relative difference between retrospective (peeled) and reference-model estimates, used to assess systematic bias in SSB and F reconstructions across retrospective peels.",
    "The mean relative difference between each peel's one-step-ahead forecast and the corresponding reference-model estimate, used to assess short-term forecasting reliability.",
    "Autocorrelation function applied to annual recruitment deviations (RecDevs). Significant autocorrelation at successive lags indicates residual temporal structure not captured by the model, suggesting misspecification of recruitment dynamics."
  ),
  Reference = c(
    "—",
    "Carvalho et al. (2021)",
    "Hyndman & Koehler (2006)",
    "Bozdogan (1987)",
    "Hurtado-Ferro et al. (2015)",
    "Hurtado-Ferro et al. (2015)",
    "Johnson et al. (2016)"
  ),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

flextable(df_model_metrics) |>
  set_caption("Diagnostic metrics used to evaluate krill stock assessment model performance") |>
  theme_booktabs() |>
  fontsize(size = 9, part = "all") |>
  font(fontname = "Arial", part = "all") |>
  bold(part = "header") |>
  autofit() |>
  set_table_properties(width = 1, layout = "autofit")
```


# Results

## Model Performance and Complexity Across Scenarios

All four scenarios achieved convergence, with a maximum gradient of $1 \times 10^{-4}$ in every case and no evidence of a non-positive-definite Hessian. Goodness-of-fit to the observed data was assessed with Pearson residuals of the predicted length distributions and with the runs test applied to all abundance-index and length-composition series (S1. Fig 11, 12), with no evident visual patterns detected in the residuals. The runs test was largely consistent with model adequacy across scenarios, with the majority of series passing (p > 0.05) in both data types. Two series showed persistent lack of fit irrespective of scenario configuration: the SSIW fishery index failed the abundance-index test in all four scenarios (p ≤ 0.03), and the EI fishery series failed the length-composition test in three of four scenarios (s1.1, s1.3, s1.4; p ≤ 0.05), passing only when predator was included alone (s1.2, p = 0.14). The BS fishery index, by contrast, passed in the baseline and environmental-only scenarios but failed specifically once the predator covariate entered the model (s1.2, s1.4; p = 0.01), and the JOIN fishery index failed only in the fully coupled scenario (s1.4, p = 0.01) — an early signal that predator inclusion, particularly in combination with the environmental term, erodes residual randomness rather than improving it uniformly (Figure \@ref(fig:runtest)).



```{r runtest, eval=TRUE, fig.cap="Runs test results for abundance indices and length compositions by index and scenario. Green cells indicate residuals consistent with random variation (Passed); red cells indicate a significant run pattern (Failed); grey cells (Excluded) indicate insufficient data to compute the test for that index/scenario combination. Labeled values are the runs test p-value (– = not data)."}
knitr::include_graphics('Figs/runstest-1.jpeg')
```

Temporal structure in recruitment deviations, assessed via the autocorrelation function (Figure \@ref(fig:acfrec)), was minimal in the baseline (s1.1) and environmental-only (s1.3) scenarios, with all lags remaining within the ±0.33 confidence bounds. The predator-only (s1.2) and, more markedly, the fully coupled (s1.4) scenarios showed elevated autocorrelation at short lags (approximately lags 1 and 5–8), with s1.4 approaching or exceeding the confidence bounds at lag 1, a first indication that recruitment estimation becomes progressively less stable as ecosystem covariates accumulate in the model.


```{r acfrec, eval=TRUE, fig.cap="Autocorrelation function (ACF) of recruitment deviations for four krill population model scenarios. Dashed lines indicate 95% confidence intervals."}
knitr::include_graphics('Figs/ACF_recruitment.png')
```


Total likelihood and its major components differed substantially among scenarios, with length-composition likelihood driving most of the difference: Length_comp_like more than doubled when the predator covariate was included (394.1 in s1.1 vs. 907.6 in s1.2; 393.1 in s1.3 vs. 948.9 in s1.4), while survey likelihood decreased slightly under the same comparison (362.0 vs. 290.2; 346.8 vs. 306.8), indicating that the added likelihood cost of predator inclusion is concentrated in the length-composition data rather than the abundance index. (S1. Fig 24; S1. Table 2). Retrospective analysis (Figure \@ref(fig:rhoplot)) made the accumulating-instability pattern explicit. Mohn's rho for SSB was near zero in the baseline ($\rho$ = −0.03), increased in magnitude with predator alone (s1.2: $\rho$ = −0.22), reversed in sign with the environmental covariate alone (s1.3: $\rho$ = 0.29), and was largest in the fully coupled scenario (s1.4: $\rho$ = −0.36). The pattern for F was considerably sharper: Mohn's rho remained low in the baseline ($\rho$ = −0.04) and of comparable, moderate magnitude with either covariate alone (s1.2: $\rho$ = −0.35; s1.3: $\rho$ = −0.43), but rose sharply and disproportionately to $\rho$ = 1.16 in s1.4 — nearly three times the magnitude observed for either single-covariate scenario, and well outside the ±0.20–0.30 reference range commonly applied to short-lived stocks. One-step-ahead forecast bias followed the same trajectory: forecast rho for SSB was comparable across the baseline and single-covariate scenarios (s1.1: −0.22; s1.2: −0.25; s1.3: 0.05) and largest in s1.4 (−0.38), while forecast rho for F stayed low in the baseline (0.05) and single-covariate scenarios (s1.2: −0.11; s1.3: −0.35) but jumped to 1.38 in s1.4, showing that retrospective instability in the fully coupled scenario propagates directly into its short-term forecasting reliability (Table \@ref(tab:diagnostics)). Taken together, the retrospective diagnostics indicate that estimation stability degrades as ecosystem covariates are added jointly, well beyond what either covariate produces on its own. The full retrospective trajectories for SSB and F across all peels and scenarios are provided in S1, Fig 15; 16.


```{r rhoplot, eval=TRUE, out.width="75%", fig.cap="Mohn's rho by scenario for spawning biomass (SSB) and fishing mortality (F). Bars show the mean Mohn's rho across retrospective peels; points show individual peel values; labels give the combined rho value per scenario"}
knitr::include_graphics('Figs/rhoplot.png')
```



Hindcast cross-validation (Figure \@ref(fig:maseplot)) told a markedly different story: predictive skill on new data, measured by MASE, was structured primarily by data source rather than by scenario complexity. Fishery data on GS and JOIN MUs showed persistently poor skill (MASE > 2, up to 9.02) across all four scenarios, while Survey data from GS remained at or below the MASE = 1 threshold in every scenario (0.59–0.87); Survey data from EI values (all < 1) were based on a single hindcast year (n.eval ≤ 2) and are not interpreted as evidence of genuine skill. Notably, MASE for BS fishery data improved substantially once the predator covariate was included (3.76–3.99 without predator vs. 1.22–1.38 with predator), while EI fishery data showed the reverse pattern, with MASE rising from below 1 (0.77–0.78) in the baseline and environmental-only scenarios to above 1 (1.52–1.68) once predator entered the model. Fleet-level hindcast retrospective forecasts for each scenario are shown in S1 Fig 18–21. Mean MASE (S1 Fig 22) increased gradually as ecosystem covariates were incorporated (2.01, 2.00, 2.04, and 2.13 for s1.1–s1.4), though these differences were not statistically significant.


```{r maseplot, eval=TRUE, out.width="75%", fig.cap="Mean Absolute Scaled Error (MASE) from hindcast cross-validation by index and scenario. Blue cells indicate MASE < 1 (better than a naive one-step-ahead forecast); red cells indicate MASE >= 1. The color scale is saturated at 5 to preserve contrast; labeled values show the true MASE. Asterisks mark indices with n.eval <= 2, too few hindcast years for a reliable skill estimate"}
knitr::include_graphics('Figs/mase-1.jpeg')
```


Consistent with these index level patterns, RMSE for the abundance indices decreased (improved) relative to the baseline in all three ecosystem-informed scenarios (s1.2: −6.0%; s1.3: −1.3%; s1.4: −3.2%), whereas RMSE for length composition increased (worsened) specifically when predator was included (s1.2: +7.7%; s1.4: +9.9%) and was unchanged in the environmental-only scenario (s1.3: +0.0%) (Figure \@ref(fig:rmseplot)).


```{r rmseplot, eval=TRUE, out.width="75%", fig.cap="Percent change in combined RMSE for abundance indices and length compositions, relative to the reference scenario (s1.1)."}
knitr::include_graphics('Figs/rmse_delta_scenarios_2.png')
```


AIC differed substantially among scenarios and was driven primarily by the inclusion of the predator covariate rather than by overall model complexity: AIC increased from 1636.9 in the baseline (s1.1) to 2531.8 once predator was added (s1.2), whereas the environmental covariate alone (s1.3, AIC = 1631.4) left model fit essentially unchanged. The fully coupled scenario (s1.4) had the highest AIC (2655.1). Together, these diagnostics converge on a consistent picture: added ecosystem realism did not uniformly erode predictive performance — hindcast skill and index-level RMSE were, if anything, comparable to or better than the baseline — but the internal stability of the estimation itself became progressively more fragile as covariates accumulated, culminating in the disproportionate retrospective and forecasting instability observed once predator and environmental effects were estimated jointly (s1.4).

Model complexity was evaluated using the Akaike Information Criterion (AIC). s1.3 provided the best parsimony-adjusted fit (1,631.4), closely followed by s1.1 (1,636.9), a difference of only 5.5 units. In contrast, s1.2 (2,531.8) and s1.4 (2,655.1) showed substantially higher AIC values despite requiring more estimated parameters (102 and 104, respectively, versus 96 in s1.1), indicating that the structural cost of incorporating predator-derived mortality, reflected in the additional parameters required to estimate time-varying $M_2$, predator selectivity, and associated deviations, was not merely unmatched by an improvement in likelihood but was accompanied by a marked deterioration in overall fit (total likelihood of 1,214.9 and 1,275.5 in s1.2 and s1.4, respectively, versus 770.5 in s1.1) (Table \@ref(tab:diagnostics)).

```{r diagnostics, eval=TRUE, warning=FALSE, message=FALSE}
diagnostics <- read_csv("outputs/model_diagnosis_results.csv")
grad_row <- which(diagnostics$Description == "Final gradient")
param_row <- which(diagnostics$Description == "No. parameters")

flextable(diagnostics) |>
  colformat_num(j      = c("s1.1", "s1.2", "s1.3", "s1.4"),
                digits = 2,
                na_str = "-") |>
  compose(
    i     = grad_row,
    j     = c("s1.1", "s1.2", "s1.3", "s1.4"),
    value = as_paragraph("<1.00e-04")
  ) |>
  compose(
    i     = param_row,
    j     = c("s1.1", "s1.2", "s1.3", "s1.4"),
    value = as_paragraph(
      as_chunk(format(as.integer(diagnostics[param_row, c("s1.1","s1.2","s1.3","s1.4")]),
                      big.mark = ""))
    )
  ) |>
  set_header_labels(Description = "Metric") |>
  set_caption("Statistical components to evaluate performance and diagnostics of model scenarios") |>
  theme_booktabs() |>
  fontsize(size = 10, part = "all") |>
  bold(part = "header") |>
  autofit() |>
  set_table_properties(width = 1, layout = "autofit")
```

## Comparison between scenarios

Krill population variables, expressed in relative terms, showed consistent temporal trends across all scenarios over the period 1989–2020, differing primarily in magnitude rather than in the direction or timing of population dynamics (Figure \@ref(fig:compara1)). Three population variables are reported: summary biomass ($B_{smry}$), which excludes individuals below the minimum summary age and represents the fraction vulnerable to surveys and the fishery; spawning stock biomass (SSB), computed at the time of peak spawning (austral summer); and age-0 recruitment. Survey-aggregated biomass estimates from the AMLR hydroacoustic Program (blue diamonds; 95% CI propagated across management units), also expressed relative to the 1989 baseline, are overlaid on the $B_{smry}$ panel, as SS3 calibrates survey catchability $q$ against this metric. All four scenarios tracked the same interannual dynamics: relatively stable biomass from 1989 to approximately 2010, punctuated by transient peaks around 1993 and 2003, followed by a marked increase peaking around 2016–2017, and a partial decline thereafter. Recruitment showed high interannual variability across all scenarios, with a pronounced, shared peak around 2014–2015. Differences among scenarios were, however, substantial in magnitude: configurations excluding predator-derived natural mortality (s1.1, s1.3) consistently produced higher relative estimates across all three variables, with summary biomass, SSB, and recruitment peaks approximately two to five times greater than those estimated under s1.2 and s1.4 (S1. Fig 10).

```{r compara1, eval=TRUE,  out.width="100%", fig.cap = "Time series of krill population variables in the Western Antarctic Peninsula (WAP), expressed relative to their 1989 value (dashed line at 1.0): summary biomass, spawning stock biomass, and recruitment (left to right). Blue diamonds represent survey biomass estimates from the AMLR Program across Subarea 48.1, also expressed relative"}
knitr::include_graphics('Figs/popvar_scenarios_relative.png')
```

This magnitude gap is directly explained by the underlying stock-recruitment dynamics, which differed consistently and biologically coherently across model configurations (Figure \@ref(fig:recpro)). Scenarios excluding predator-derived natural mortality (s1.1, s1.3) produced substantially higher asymptotic recruitment curves (~40–45 billion individuals), with predicted values remaining elevated even at low spawning biomass levels, indicating high compensatory productivity under these assumptions (Figure \@ref(fig:recpro)A). In contrast, configurations incorporating the $M_2$ predator term (s1.2, s1.4) yielded markedly lower and more saturating stock-recruitment curves (~10–15 billion), implying reduced population productivity when predation mortality is explicitly accounted for. Recruitment efficiency (R/SSB) as a function of relative spawning biomass (SSB/SSB$_0$) followed the same grouping: s1.1 and s1.3 consistently exhibited higher per-capita productivity across all depletion levels, whereas s1.2 and s1.4 showed substantially lower efficiency, particularly at low SSB (Figure \@ref(fig:recpro)B). The virgin recruitment parameter ln($R_0$) confirms this pattern: s1.1 and s1.3 estimate higher unfished recruitment (~24.3–24.5), whereas s1.2 and s1.4 converge on lower values (~23.4–23.6), with s1.4 showing the most precise estimate (narrowest posterior density) (Figure \@ref(fig:recpro)C). Together, these results indicate that the two- to five-fold difference in biomass and recruitment magnitude observed across scenarios (Figure \@ref(fig:compara1)) originates primarily from differences in estimated productivity rather than from divergent population trajectories, with predator-derived mortality acting as the dominant structural driver of this contrast.

```{r recpro, eval=TRUE,  out.width="100%", fig.cap = "Stock–recruitment relationships (A), recruitment efficiency (B), and posterior distribution of ln(R0) (C) for Antarctic krill under four assessment scenarios. Beverton–Holt curves fitted to observed SSB–recruitment pairs; panel B shows per-capita productivity (R/SSB) as a function of relative spawning biomass (SSB/SSB\\textsubscript{0}); panel C shows the marginal posterior of virgin recruitment."}
knitr::include_graphics('Figs/fig_recpro2.png')
```

# Discussion


This study advances understanding of Antarctic krill (*Euphausia superba*) population dynamics by addressing two fundamental objectives. It consolidates and harmonizes multiple long-term datasets collected over decades, particularly from Subarea 48.1 in the WAP, into a unified statistical framework, responding to a recurrent management priority regarding integrated models for krill emphasized by CCAMLR. Additionally, it integrates ecosystem variables such as environmental drivers and predator impacts, thereby moving beyond the traditional single-stock approach and taking a step toward ecosystem-informed stock assessments. This approach not only enhances the biological realism of krill population modeling but also reveals the structural complexity and statistical challenges that must be addressed for its effective application in Antarctic fishery management contexts.

Previous integrated assessments of Antarctic krill have progressively advanced the structural complexity of population models, moving from age-structured formulations [@Kinzey2015] to size-structured frameworks [@Wang2021; @Green2023; @Zhang2022; @Dong2025], all implemented within Stock Synthesis or analogous platforms. Despite these advances, two fundamental limitations persist across this body of work. First, these assessments have relied on a restricted set of input data, typically conditioned on acoustic survey indices and fishery catch, without simultaneously incorporating fishery-dependent size compositions, standardized CPUE, predator abundance indices, diet-derived size selectivity, and environmental covariates within the same likelihood framework. Second, and more critically, ecosystem drivers such as environmental variability and predator pressure have been treated as external to the core population dynamics, explored through sensitivity analyses or post-hoc diagnostics rather than embedded structurally within the equations governing recruitment and natural mortality. As a result, their influence on estimated stock status and management advice has remained indirect and largely non-binding. The present study departs from both limitations: it conditions the model simultaneously on the full breadth of available data streams, fishery-dependent data, acoustic survey indices, a primary productivity covariate linked to recruitment, and penguin abundance and diet composition informing predation mortality — and embeds these ecosystem components directly within the state equations. This dual integration, of data sources and ecological structure, represents the primary methodological contribution of this work and the key distinction from all previous krill assessments.

Embedding ecosystem drivers directly within the state equations, rather than treating them as external covariates, exposes the model to their full statistical cost, a consequence largely avoided by the post-hoc or sensitivity-based treatments that have historically kept ecosystem information non-binding in tactical fisheries management [@SkernMauritzen2016]. As detailed in the sections that follow, this cost is measurable and, in places, substantial, echoing similar trade-offs reported when environmentally driven productivity is embedded structurally in other assessed stocks [@Haltuch2009; @Crone2019]. We interpret it not as evidence against the underlying ecological mechanisms, independently supported by an extensive literature on krill–environment and krill–predator relationships, but as the expected outcome of a first attempt to formalize this integration, identifying targets for future development rather than undermining the case for ecosystem-informed assessment.


## Spatial Considerations and the Areas-as-Fleets Approach

Recognizing and accounting for spatial heterogeneity in krill populations across Subarea 48.1 was essential for the integrated model design, a structure particularly appropriate given the well-documented spatial variability in population processes and fishing effort across the WAP, including known differences in size composition among MUs [@Kinzey2011; @Reiss2020; @Cutter2022]. The areas-as-fleets approach captures spatial differences in abundance, selectivity, and population processes, allowing their incorporation into global population estimates [@Nielsen2021; @Waterhouse2014]. However, some MUs, particularly Joinville Island, had limited survey and fishery monitoring data, which could introduce complications in future integrated krill modeling efforts. Moving toward spatially explicit integrated models represents the natural next step — efforts in this direction already exist from alternative modeling perspectives, including spatially resolved models incorporating movement and age structure [@Kinzey2011], ecosystem-dynamics approaches linking spatial structure to predator-fishery interactions [@Watters2013], and habitat-driven mechanistic frameworks such as KRILLPODYM [@Green2023]. Fully integrating this spatial resolution within an assessment framework would allow movement, local depletion, and habitat-driven heterogeneity to be represented directly within the population dynamics rather than absorbed by fleet-specific parameters. State-space frameworks such as SAM [@Nielsen2021] and WHAM [@Stock2021] offer structural advantages in this direction, particularly in their capacity to partition process and observation uncertainty and to accommodate time-varying spatial effects. However, both frameworks rely on age-structured population dynamics and require age-composition data for reliable process error estimation, a fundamental constraint for krill, given the absence of hard aging structures amenable to routine, large-scale sampling, notwithstanding recent methodological advances in krill ageing [@Kilada2017], and the resulting infeasibility of age-based sampling at assessment scales [@Kinzey2015; @Nicol2000]. Spatially explicit implementation for krill therefore remains contingent on advances in aging methodology or the development of length-structured state-space extensions capable of resolving spatial population processes without relying on age data.


## Ecosystems drivers and krill populations dynamics

As expected, Chl-a concentration emerged as a main environmental driver of krill recruitment, highlighting the central role of primary productivity in shaping population dynamics [@Constable2023; @Saba2014]. This finding is consistent with studies emphasizing that krill recruitment is primarily driven by environmental conditions rather than spawning stock biomass [@ichii2023; @Perry2020; @Veytia2021; @McBride2021]. It is worth noting, however, that the literature on krill–environment relationships is extensive and, in some cases, contradictory: the effects of sea ice, temperature, and primary productivity on krill abundance and recruitment have been reported as positive, negative, or nonlinear depending on the season, life stage, spatial scale, and analytical approach considered [@McBride2021; @Kawaguchi2024; @Dong2025]. These discrepancies reflect the complexity of the mechanisms linking environmental variability to krill population dynamics and caution against overreliance on any single covariate or linear functional form. By explicitly incorporating variables mechanistically linked to recruitment, stock assessment models move beyond purely stochastic representations of stock productivity [@Haltuch2009; @Crone2019].

The absence of predictive improvement in s1.3 relative to s1.1 in terms of MASE does not imply ecological irrelevance of primary productivity as a recruitment driver, but rather that the additive Z-scored link as currently parameterised does not translate that relationship into improved predictive capacity. Similar limitations have been noted in ecosystem-informed stock assessments where environmental covariates are incorporated within the stock-recruitment function: @Crone2019 found that including environmental data as a parameter of the spawner-recruit relationship produces greater bias in key assessment outputs than using it as an external index, a result consistent with the near-identical predictive performance of s1.3 and s1.1 observed here. In SS3 specifically, recruitment deviations absorb environmental forcing when estimated simultaneously with covariate links, further diluting the identifiable contribution of the covariate [@Punt2014]. State-space models such as WHAM [@Stock2021] explicitly partition process and observation uncertainty, allowing environmental covariates to act on latent state variables without competing with random effects, an architecture shown to improve retrospective diagnostics and covariate identifiability in ecosystem-informed assessments [@Kittel2026]. However, this same age-data constraint discussed above currently precludes applying WHAM's architecture to krill. Future studies should consider multivariate environmental relationships, threshold effects, and lagged responses that may better represent mechanistic links between climate variability and krill population dynamics [@Kawaguchi2024].

The integration of penguin predation data into natural mortality estimates represents a novel approach in an integrated stock assessment for krill. The size-selective predation pattern incorporated is biologically consistent with foraging theory and observed predator behaviour [@Panasiuk2024]. The declining trend in the synoptic predator biomass index after 2015 reflects documented population declines in Antarctic Peninsula penguin colonies [@Kruger2019; @Salmeron2023; @Trivelpiece2011a], attributed to climate change impacts, sea ice loss, and shifts in prey availability [@Kruger2019]. The incorporation of this declining predation pressure provides a mechanism for capturing ecosystem-mediated changes in natural mortality that would otherwise be overlooked in traditional single-species approaches [@Richards2016].

Incorporating predation mortality into stock assessment models has precedent in the literature. @Hollowed2000 revealed higher total natural mortality rates than traditional life-history estimates and showed that ignoring predation uncertainty underestimated stock biomass uncertainty by up to 20%. Similarly, @Richards2016 introduced a predation pressure index for northern shrimp, combining predator biomass and diet frequency to scale natural mortality over time, improving model fit and reducing retrospective bias without requiring absolute predator consumption data. Within the krill assessment literature, @Deehr2024 explored time-varying natural and fishing mortality in the GRYM framework at the within-year scale, incorporating seasonal patterns of predator presence at daily timesteps; their results showed that intra-annual variation in M increased precautionary catch limits. The present study extends this concept to the inter-annual scale, parameterizing annual log-scale deviations in predation mortality across 1979–2020. Despite this, penguin predation almost certainly represents a conservative lower bound on total predation pressure in the WAP. Crabeater seals feed almost exclusively on krill; in the WAP–western Weddell Sea region alone, their annual consumption has been estimated at 12.26 million tonnes (95% CI: 8.12–18.61) [@Forcada2012], already exceeding both commercial catch and penguin consumption combined in the same area. Baleen whales add further pressure through direct competition with the fishery [@Reisinger2022; @Biuw2024; @Savoca2024], and whale reproductive rates are themselves linked to interannual krill availability [@Pallin2023]. Integrating these predators into the M2 framework faces a fundamental data constraint: available consumption estimates derive largely from point studies rather than continuous, multi-decadal time series of abundance and diet composition comparable to the MAPPPD penguin dataset. The penguin exercise demonstrates that structural integration is achievable when an adequate index exists. Critically, what the model requires is not absolute consumption but a temporally coherent relative index, since predation mortality is scaled through an estimable catchability parameter *Q* and it is the trend, not the magnitude, that drives the M2 signal [@methot2020stock]. Extending this approach to whales and seals therefore depends on developing continuous, spatially resolved monitoring programs that provide the temporal contrast needed for reliable parameter estimation.

The systematic divergence between predator-inclusive and predator-exclusive krill model scenarios confirms that top-down predation pressure exerts a stronger and more continuous influence on estimated krill biomass than the environmental covariate, which operates episodically through recruitment [@Atkinson2004; @Murphy2007]. When predator mortality is absent, the model attributes the full signal in survey indices to population growth, inflating biomass and recruitment estimates, an effect particularly evident in the 2015–2016 peaks, which reflect anomalously favourable environmental conditions [@Siegel2005] but are amplified when predation-driven removal is not accounted for. 

## Model Performance and Diagnostic Evaluation

All scenarios achieved convergence and produced stable Hessian matrices, confirming that the increasing structural complexity of ecosystem-informed configurations did not compromise numerical stability. The comprehensive diagnostic evaluation, however, revealed important and consistent trade-offs between biological realism and statistical performance [@Collie2016; @Robertson2024]. Consistent with the structural cost anticipated at the outset, these trade-offs are interpreted throughout this section as the expected consequence of formalizing ecosystem drivers within the state equations for the first time, rather than as evidence against the mechanisms themselves.

Pearson residual misfits concentrated among larger size classes in several Bransfield Strait survey fleets suggest that the current spatially implicit model structure may not fully resolve the processes governing adult krill abundance and selectivity in this sub-region. The Bransfield Strait has been consistently identified as a core juvenile habitat [@Mardones2025; @Veytia2021; @Perry2020; @Perry2019], implying that adult individuals are disproportionately distributed elsewhere. Incorporating explicit spatial structure in future assessments could reduce these residual patterns by allowing size-selective processes to vary across MUs. Similarly, persistent residuals in the largest size classes of the predator fleet reflect limitations in the time-invariant logistic selectivity function applied to penguin predation, which may inadequately capture temporal shifts in prey size preferences [@Marin2001; @Silvestro2023].

Based on AIC, s1.3 provided the best parsimony-adjusted fit (1,631.4), closely followed by s1.1 (1,636.9), while s1.2 (2,531.8) and s1.4 (2,655.1) showed substantially higher values — a $\Delta$AIC exceeding 894 units relative to the base model (894.9 for s1.2, 1,018.2 for s1.4), well beyond conventional significance thresholds [@Burnham2002] — indicating that the addition of predator-derived mortality incurred a considerable informational cost not offset by improved overall fit. This pattern was driven primarily by length composition likelihoods, which were markedly lower in s1.1 and s1.3 (~393–394) than in s1.2 and s1.4 (~908–949), indicating substantially poorer fit to length frequency data in predator-inclusive configurations. In contrast, survey likelihood was lowest in s1.2 (290.2) and s1.4 (306.8), suggesting that predator scenarios achieved better alignment with abundance index trends despite their overall poorer fit. This divergence between compositional and index fit is consistent with the risk of overfitting compositional data at the expense of capturing the broader population trajectory [@Punt2013; @Maunder2013], and reflects a fundamental tension between data types in integrated assessments. It should be noted, however, that AIC comparisons across model configurations fitted to non-identical data streams, as is the case here, where predator-inclusive scenarios incorporate additional observational components, should be interpreted with caution, since differences in the likelihood basis partly reflect data structure rather than model parsimony alone [@Carvalho2021b].

The hindcast cross-validation diagnostic provides a robust framework for comparing model configurations beyond in-sample goodness-of-fit metrics [@Carvalho2021]. Mean MASE values exceeded 1.0 in all four scenarios (2.72, 2.11, 2.73, and 2.29 for s1.1–s1.4, respectively), reflecting the extreme interannual variability inherent in Antarctic krill abundance [@Atkinson2004; @Everson2000] and representing a fundamental challenge for any deterministic assessment framework; indices with lower intrinsic variability, such as the Elephant Island (SURVEYEI) and Gerlache Strait (SURVEYGS) surveys, nonetheless achieved MASE below 1.0 across all four configurations. The persistent poor predictive performance of the Gerlache Strait fishery index is consistent with the known spatial aggregation behaviour of krill, which generates high variability in fishery-dependent indices difficult to capture through model structure alone [@Everson2000; @Constable2000], though its MASE nearly halved under predator-inclusive configurations (≈9.0 in s1.1/s1.3 versus ≈4.6–5.2 in s1.2/s1.4). This improvement, however, is not general across fleets: while FISHERYBS and SURVEYBS (Bransfield Strait) also showed better predictive skill under s1.2 and s1.4, FISHERYJOIN (Joinville Island), FISHERYSSIW (South Shetland Islands West), and SURVEYGS showed the opposite pattern, with MASE increasing under predator-inclusive configurations. Rather than a uniform gain in predictive skill, this fleet-specific pattern suggests that temporally structured variation in $M_2$, informed by MAPPPD penguin abundance indices, redistributes predictive accuracy across management units rather than improving it evenly, consistent with the role of top-down predator control in structuring krill dynamics unevenly across space and timescales [@Trivelpiece2011a; @Constable2000].

The deterioration in retrospective performance in ecosystem-informed scenarios reflects the informational cost incurred when predator and environmental drivers are embedded directly within the state equations. The extreme instability of F estimates in s1.4 (Mohn's $\rho$ = 1.157) is consistent with identifiability constraints arising from the joint estimation of time-varying predation and fishing mortality from the same population signal. This spike suggests that the 2017 peel year is a leverage point for the joint ecosystem configuration, likely reflecting the sensitivity of F estimation to the interaction between predator-driven mortality and environmental recruitment signals in a data-limited peel context. The SSB $\rho$ in s1.3 (0.290) sits just below the relaxed threshold proposed for short-lived species (ρ > 0.30) [@HurtadoF2015], indicating comparatively modest retrospective sensitivity to the environmental link — a milder pattern than the pronounced instability observed in s1.4's F estimates. In interpreting these values, acceptable thresholds for Mohn's $\rho$ are not universal: @HurtadoF2015 proposed relaxed bounds for short-lived species compared to longer-lived species, reflecting the greater natural variability characteristic of fast-turnover populations — bounds that may need to be interpreted with additional latitude for a species such as krill, whose interannual variability in recruitment and biomass substantially exceeds that of most assessed stocks. More fundamentally, @Cadrin2025 argues that retrospective patterns should not be interpreted as a measure of estimation bias amenable to correction: they are informative diagnostics that identify model misspecification, and when they cannot be reduced through respecification, they should be communicated as a measure of uncertainty for consideration in precautionary management. This framing is directly applicable here — the retrospective pattern observed in s1.4 is not evidence against the ecological relevance of the incorporated drivers, but rather reflects the structural tension between imposing ecosystem constraints and the informational capacity of the available data. Communicated transparently as uncertainty, it strengthens rather than undermines the precautionary basis of the assessment.


Autocorrelated recruitment deviations in s1.4 indicate that this configuration failed to fully capture the underlying drivers of interannual recruitment variability [@Thorson2014; @jhonson2016]. When both $M_2(t)$ and $\beta_E E_t$ are estimated jointly, collinearity between ecosystem drivers prevents the optimiser from cleanly partitioning mortality and recruitment signals, forcing recruitment deviations to compensate for unresolved variance. This pattern reinforces the interpretation that s1.4 incurs a higher informational cost and poorer internal consistency than simpler configurations, and suggests that disentangling predation and environmental recruitment signals may require either sequential estimation approaches or state-space architectures that explicitly partition these sources of variance [@Stock2021; @Kittel2026].


## Implications for Precautionary Management

Two patterns in Figure \@ref(fig:compara1) warrant brief clarification before turning to their management implications. The apparent discrepancy between raw survey totals and model-estimated $B_{smry}$ is expected: an estimated $q > 1$ indicates that surveys sampled areas of above-average krill density relative to the stock-wide mean [@Everson2000; @Siegel2005], a spatial bias resolved internally within the SS3 likelihood framework rather than reflecting an absolute stock estimate; SSB may likewise exceed $B_{smry}$ in years of rapid somatic growth between the start of the year and the spawning event, consistent with the fast growth rates characteristic of Antarctic krill [@Atkinson2006]. The high interannual variability in recruitment is itself consistent with the episodic, environmentally driven nature of krill recruitment [@Dornam2021; @Dong2025], and the fact that these common trends, including the shared 2014–2015 recruitment peak, are reproduced across all four model structures indicates that the underlying population signal is robust regardless of how ecosystem drivers are incorporated into the state equations: what differs between scenarios is magnitude, not direction.

That magnitude, however, is where the ecosystem-informed configurations carry direct management weight. Despite their comparatively weaker statistical performance, s1.2 and s1.4 consistently yield lower estimates of summary biomass, spawning biomass, and recruitment (Figure \@ref(fig:compara1)), and this is not an isolated biomass artefact: the same divergence traces back to lower estimated productivity, evident in the flatter stock-recruitment curves, reduced recruitment efficiency, and lower virgin recruitment ln($R_0$) under predator-inclusive scenarios (Figure \@ref(fig:recpro)). Neglecting these ecosystem drivers therefore does not merely shift a single output metric; it propagates through the productivity relationship itself, risking the kind of overly optimistic stock assessment that non-binding treatment of ecosystem processes has been shown to produce elsewhere [@SkernMauritzen2016]. This conservative tendency aligns with CCAMLR's strategic guidance to integrate ecosystem variables into predictive models supporting precautionary management [@Constable2011; @Cavanagh2016; @Constable2023], a gap CCAMLR has explicitly recognized alongside the absence of a formal stock assessment process and of spatial components in current management recommendations [@Hill2016; @Hill2019; @Watters2013; @Warwick-Evans2022]. The present framework could directly addresses the stock assessment component of the strategy under development, providing a scientific basis for precautionary catch limit estimation. As @Watters2013 argued, a candid appraisal of uncertainty, expressed as risk rather than as a single point estimate, aids rather than hinders decision-making in ecosystem-based krill management; the systematically lower, productivity-linked estimates from ecosystem-informed configurations are precisely the kind of precautionary signal such risk-based frameworks are designed to accommodate, particularly given the high variability and unpredictability of Antarctic marine ecosystems [@Hill2016]. This is especially relevant in a spatial context: @Warwick-Evans2022 identified the current distribution of krill fishing effort in Subarea 48.1 as carrying some of the highest ecosystem risk in the fishery. The consequences of losing spatial control were immediate: following the 2024 expiration of Conservation Measure 51-07, which had allocated catches among subareas, catches in Subarea 48.1 more than doubled within months, from 0.155 to 0.355 Mt by July 2025 [@Meyer2025]. This is compounded by the fact that the operational 0.62 Mt catch limit for Area 48 is itself derived from historical catch levels rather than current stock size, while the much larger 5.61 Mt precautionary limit it was meant to approximate still rests on a single biomass survey conducted in Area 48 in 2000, covering only ~57% of the fishing area [@Meyer2025], underscoring, as @Meyer2025 themselves argue in proposing a dynamic Krill Stock Hypothesis integrating recruitment, spatial connectivity, and predator dynamics, the urgency of assessment tools able to represent these processes jointly rather than relying on a quarter-century-old snapshot. The increased model complexity this requires, and the statistical challenges it brings, must nonetheless be weighed against the gain in biological realism to keep management advice both scientifically credible and operationally feasible.

## Model Limitations and Future Directions

Several limitations of the current modelling approach warrant discussion. The integration of predator effects relied on relatively coarse-scale abundance indices that may not fully capture fine-scale predator-prey interactions across the whole of Subarea 48.1, where CEMP, for instance, does not provide spatially comprehensive coverage. The current model also assumes static relationships between ecosystem variables and parameter estimates, which may be altered by climate change over time, requiring adaptive modelling approaches that can accommodate non-stationary ecosystem conditions [@Constable2023]. The development of time-varying parameter frameworks or regime-specific models may be necessary to address this challenge. Performance and diagnostic limitations reflect the inherent cost of imposing ecosystem structure within a spatially implicit, single-region assessment framework. Rather than indicating fundamental model failure, they identify specific processes — spatial heterogeneity in size structure and temporally dynamic predation selectivity — that represent natural targets for future model development. Despite these limitations, this study represents a forward-looking direction for integrated krill assessments: it is, to our knowledge, among the first to formally embed both environmental and predator-derived mortality within the state equations of a krill stock assessment, offering a scientifically grounded, if still developing, foundation for recommendations to CCAMLR as the Commission moves toward more dynamic, ecosystem-informed management approaches [@Meyer2025].

\newpage


# Conclusion

This study demonstrates that integrating ecosystem variables into Antarctic krill stock assessment models produces measurable and consistent effects on key population variables, with potential implications for management advice. By harmonizing diverse long-term datasets within a spatially implicit integrated framework and embedding environmental and predator covariates directly within the state equations, we show that the explicit representation of ecosystem components generates systematic and coherent differences in estimated population variables. Predation-derived natural mortality emerged as the dominant structural driver of these differences, producing substantially lower and more conservative estimates of summary biomass, spawning biomass, and recruitment relative to configurations that excluded top-down control, while environmental forcing through primary productivity exerted a comparatively weaker but non-negligible influence, primarily modulating interannual variability in recruitment rather than shifting its mean level. Together, these results indicate that the choice of which ecosystem components to embed within the core population dynamics, and how, determines not only the magnitude but also the temporal structure of estimated stock status, and support CCAMLR's precautionary management principles by suggesting that assessments excluding ecosystem processes may overestimate population productivity and stock status. The lapse of Conservation Measure 51-07 in 2024 and the subsequent doubling of catches in Subarea 48.1 by July 2025 [@Meyer2025] underscore the timeliness of assessment frameworks that can credibly represent ecosystem dynamics and support spatially explicit, precautionary harvest decisions in this region.
